sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ὤρνυτ’ ἄρ’ ἐξ εὐνῆφι βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
εἵματα ἑσσάμενος, περὶ δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ θέτ’ ὤμῳ,
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
up rose from his bed, good at the war-cry, Menelaus,
his clothes having put on, and round, a sharp sword he set on his shoulder,
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, up rose from his bed Menelaus, good at the war-cry, and he put on his clothes and slung a sharp sword about his shoulder,
sentences.n: This whole couplet repeats, almost word for word, the formulaic dawn-and-arming lines already shipped in odyssey-005 (2.1–2), where the subject was Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός ’Odysseus’ dear son’; here only the subject changes, to βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος, the house-fixed epithet ’good at the war-cry’. ὤρνυτ’ is ὤρνυτο, an UNaugmented imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι ’rise’ (root ὀρ-νυ-), not an aorist. ἑσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἕννυμι ’clothe’; περὶ … θέτ’ is tmesis for περιέθετο. εὐνῆφι carries the old case-suffix -φι, ablatival, ’from his bed’.

sentences.t:
ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο θεῷ ἐναλίγκιος ἄντην,
Τηλεμάχῳ δὲ παρῖζεν, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
and under his sleek feet he bound fine sandals,
and set out to go from the chamber, like to a god to look upon,
and beside Telemachus he sat, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: he bound fine sandals beneath his sleek feet, went out of his chamber like a god to look upon, sat down beside Telemachus, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: Lines 309–310 reuse, unchanged, the couplet already shipped word for word in odyssey-005 (2.4–5), there too of a man arming at dawn; there it closed the sentence with a full stop, but here the sentence runs on into 311, so the same Greek carries a comma instead. ἐδήσατο is an AUGMENTED aorist middle (contrast the unaugmented ὤρνυτ’ just above); ὑπὸ … ἐδήσατο is tmesis. παρῖζεν is an imperfect of παρίζω, its augment hidden inside the long ῑ. The closing phrase ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν matches the house table’s fixed rendering of this address-formula (‘spoke a word, and called him by name’).

sentences.t:
τίπτε δέ σε χρειὼ δεῦρ’ ἤγαγε, Τηλέμαχ’ ἥρως,
ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν, ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης;
sentences.l:
“Why then has need brought you here, Telemachus, hero,
to heavenly Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
sentences.i: “Why has necessity brought you here, hero Telemachus, to heavenly Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε contracted, ’why ever’. χρειώ ’need, necessity’ is treated as the grammatical agent of ἤγαγε, an AUGMENTED aorist of ἄγω (ἠ- from ἀ-). ἥρως, vocative in direct address to Telemachus, is the house-fixed title ’the hero’ (already used generically), here simply ’hero’. Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν is the house-fixed ’heavenly Lacedaemon’. νῶτα θαλάσσης, ’the back(s) of the sea’, uses the poetic plural νῶτα for a single stretch of open water. This opens Menelaus’s question and Murray’s next paragraph.

sentences.i: Is this a public matter, or a private one?
sentences.n: δήμιον and ἴδιον are neuter adjectives standing for an unspoken noun (something like πρῆγμα ’matter, business’), each agreeing with it in turn; the same antithesis, ’private, not public’, was Telemachus’s own description of his errand to Nestor at 3.82 (odyssey-009: πρῆξις δ’ ἥδ’ ἰδίη, οὐ δήμιος), and Menelaus now puts it to him as a question. ἦ here is the disjunctive interrogative particle ’or’, to be told apart from asseverative ἦ ’truly’ and from ἦ ’(he/she) spoke’.

sentences.l: tell me this, the unerring truth.”
sentences.i: tell me the unerring truth of it.”
sentences.n: ἐνίσπες is an aorist imperative of the defective verb ἐνέπω/ἐνίσπω ’tell, declare’, the same verb as ἔννεπε at 1.1. With νημερτές ’unerring’ (νη- + the root of ἁμαρτάνω ’miss the mark’) it forms the recurring idiom ’tell me the unerring truth’, heard again in Telemachus’s own mouth at the very end of this part (331). τόδε ’this’ picks up the alternative just posed. The closing ” falls here: Menelaus’s question, opened at 312, is now complete, and Telemachus answers next.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This whole line is the house-fixed reply-formula for Telemachus (already shipped three times, with τόν, in odyssey-004), reused here unchanged; πεπνυμένος ’prudent’ is his standing epithet throughout the poem. Plain narration, no speech-mark of its own: it only introduces the words that follow. It also opens Murray’s next paragraph, the last of this part.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ἤλυθον, εἴ τινά μοι κληηδόνα πατρὸς ἐνίσποις.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’ son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
I have come, in case some tidings of my father you might tell me.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, I have come, in the hope that you might tell me some news of my father.
sentences.n: The vocative line reuses the house-fixed rendering already shipped for this same address (also used by Telemachus of Menelaus earlier in this very part, at line 291 of the preceding slice). ἤλυθον is an UNAUGMENTED aorist (= Attic ἦλθον, root ἐλυθ-/ἐλθ-), not to be mistaken for an augmented form. κληηδών is the Ionic by-form of κληδών ’report, rumor’ (built on the root of κλέος, κλύω). ἐνίσποις, an aorist optative of the same defective verb seen as an imperative at 314 (ἐνίσπες), with εἴ makes a wishful condition, ’in case you might tell’. This opens Telemachus’s own plea, left running to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
ἐσθίεταί μοι οἶκος, ὄλωλε δὲ πίονα ἔργα,
δυσμενέων δ’ ἀνδρῶν πλεῖος δόμος, οἵ τέ μοι αἰεὶ
μῆλ’ ἁδινὰ σφάζουσι καὶ εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς,
μητρὸς ἐμῆς μνηστῆρες ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
My house is being eaten up, and my rich estate is ruined,
and of hostile men the house is full, who for me always
thronging sheep slaughter, and rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle,
suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence.
sentences.i: My house is being eaten up, and my rich estate is ruined; the house is full of hostile men, who are always slaughtering my thronging sheep and the cattle of rolling gait and crumpled horn — suitors of my mother, with their overweening insolence.
sentences.n: ἐσθίεταί is present passive, a vivid ’is being eaten up’ even now; ὄλωλε is the perfect of ὄλλυμι, ’stands ruined’. οἵ τε carries the epic τε of a standing, habitual fact. Line 320 repeats 1.90 word for word, and both μῆλ’ ἁδινά ’thronging sheep’ and εἰλίποδας ἕλικας βοῦς ’rolling-gaited, crumple-horned cattle’ are house-fixed renderings already shipped there, reused unchanged. Line 321 opens with words Telemachus himself already used of the suitors, addressing them directly, at 1.368 (odyssey-004): ’suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence’, reused verbatim here, now spoken of them rather than to them.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ’ ἱκάνομαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα
κείνου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ἐνισπεῖν, εἴ που ὄπωπας
ὀφθαλμοῖσι τεοῖσιν ἢ ἄλλου μῦθον ἄκουσας
πλαζομένου·
sentences.l:
Therefore now to your knees I come, in case you may be willing
of that man the bitter destruction to tell, if somewhere you saw it
with your own eyes, or from another heard the tale,
a wanderer;
sentences.i: That is why I have come now to your knees, in the hope that you may be willing to tell me of his bitter destruction, if you perhaps saw it with your own eyes, or heard the tale from some other wanderer;
sentences.n: These four lines reuse, word for word, the wording already shipped for the identical Greek at 3.92–95 (odyssey-009), where Telemachus made the same plea to Nestor: Homer has him repeat it almost verbatim to a second host. Coming to a man’s knees is the suppliant’s gesture. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα uses the old 2nd-person subjunctive ending -σθα. ἄκουσας is UNAUGMENTED (Attic ἤκουσας), taking the genitive ἄλλου. πλαζομένου, ’wandering’, agrees with ἄλλου, ’some other wanderer’.

sentences.t: περὶ γάρ μιν ὀιζυρὸν τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.l: for beyond all others his mother bore him to misery.
sentences.i: for his mother bore him to more misery than any other man.
sentences.n: This clause reuses, unchanged, the English already shipped for the identical Greek at 3.95 (odyssey-009), the tail end of the same repeated plea. περί, with the accent thrown back in Homer’s usual practice (though printed περί rather than πέρι here), is the adverb ’beyond all, exceedingly’. μιν is Odysseus; τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω (Attic ἔτεκε), ’bore’.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τί μ’ αἰδόμενος μειλίσσεο μηδ’ ἐλεαίρων,
ἀλλ’ εὖ μοι κατάλεξον ὅπως ἤντησας ὀπωπῆς.
sentences.l:
And do not at all, out of respect, soften things for me, nor out of pity,
but recount to me well how you came upon the sight.
sentences.i: Do not soften anything for me out of respect or pity, but tell me plainly how you came to see it.
sentences.n: This couplet again reuses, unchanged, the English already shipped for the identical Greek at 3.96–97 (odyssey-009); the second line is also a house-fixed rendering in its own right. αἰδόμενος is ’out of respect, from delicacy’ (from αἴδομαι); ἐλεαίρων is the epic by-form of ἐλεέω ’pity’. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω; ἤντησας is an AUGMENTED aorist (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-), ’you met with’, governing the genitive ὀπωπῆς ’the sight’.

sentences.t:
λίσσομαι, εἴ ποτέ τοί τι πατὴρ ἐμός, ἐσθλὸς Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἢ ἔπος ἠέ τι ἔργον ὑποστὰς ἐξετέλεσσε
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ’ Ἀχαιοί,
τῶν νῦν μοι μνῆσαι, καί μοι νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες.
sentences.l:
I beseech you, if ever for you my father, good Odysseus,
either a word or some deed having promised, fulfilled it
in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans,
of these things now for me be mindful, and tell me the unerring truth.
sentences.i: I beseech you, if ever my father, good Odysseus, promised you some word or deed and made it good in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes, remember it now for my sake, and tell me the unerring truth.
sentences.n: This whole four-line plea reuses, word for word, the wording Telemachus used, verbatim, to Nestor at 3.98–101 (odyssey-009) — the same request repeated to a second host. λίσσομαι ’I beseech’ grounds the appeal in a past service; ὑποστάς (aor. part. of ὑφίστημι) is ’having promised’; ἐξετέλεσσε keeps its augment (ἐξ-ε-τέλεσσε) though πάσχετε beside it is unaugmented (= ἐπάσχετε). Unlike at 3.101, the speech does NOT close here: Telemachus is still speaking when this part ends, so no closing ” is given — his plea to Menelaus stays open, to be closed only when a future part (odyssey-017) resumes it, exactly as odyssey-014’s last open speech was closed only in odyssey-015.
